19897-riley-love-lyrics:
James Whitcomb Riley published Riley Love Lyrics in 1883. The Hoosier poet's love poems speak in dialect and plain English alike. One lover finds extra flavor in memory's mellow wine. A little dust of harm, he says, spices the good. He drinks the deeper to that old sweetheart of his. Riley's sentiment is open, musical, and unembarrassed.

Riley was America's most popular poet of his day. His readings filled halls from Indiana to both coasts. Love Lyrics gathers his courtship and remembrance verses. Dialect poems made his fame, but these lyrics show his range. He sings of first loves remembered in middle age. The book is a keepsake from poetry's popular age.
19985-the-dyeing-of-woollen-fabrics:
Franklin Beech wrote The Dyeing of Woollen Fabrics as a conveniently arranged handbook. He aims to supply the working dyer of wool with sound practice. Various branches of the wool dyeing industry get their own treatment. Beech trusts the book will meet the want it addresses. That want was real: dye houses guarded recipes jealously. A printed handbook put trade knowledge on any dyer's shelf.

Beech was a manufacturing chemist writing at synthetic dye's high tide. Natural dyes were yielding to aniline colors in the mills. Wool takes dye differently from cotton or silk, fiber by fiber. His recipes cover mordants, levels, and fastness in workshop terms. The book documents industrial chemistry at bench level. Textile historians still consult such manuals.
20125-a-preface-to-politics:
Walter Lippmann published A Preface to Politics in 1913, his first book, written in his twenties. He attacks a politics stuck on small points of past blame. One case turns on the campaign of 1904 and Theodore Roosevelt. The Senate chased exact guilt in an eight-year-old funds question.

Meanwhile, Lippmann argues, the nation's real needs get no thought at all. He calls for leaders who face new facts with fresh minds. The book made his name as a bold young thinker. Readers still use it to see how modern American political writing began.
20433-women-and-politics:
Women and Politics argues the case about women's place in public life by looking backward first. Its pages survey what earlier ages taught about women. The old charges are set out plainly so the reader can judge them.

Medieval writers, the book notes, blamed women for wild and unbridled passions. They claimed women fell more easily into heresy and witchcraft, and drew attacks from demons, above all if they had beautiful hair. By showing how absurd the old case was, the book clears ground for its claims about women's rights in modern politics.
22105-christianity-and-ethics-a-handbook:
Archibald B. D. Alexander wrote Christianity and Ethics as a handbook for students and clergy. He opens with Matthew Arnold's saying that conduct is three-fourths of life. If conduct matters that much, Alexander argues, its laws deserve careful study. The book asks what Christ's teaching requires of people in daily choices.

Chapters work through duty, character, family, business, and the state. Alexander writes as a teacher, defining terms and answering objections in order. He aims to join theology to ordinary morals without cant. Handbooks like this one trained ministers and lay readers to reason about right and wrong in a changing, industrial world.
22157-lectures-on-stellar-statistics:
Carl Charlier, the Swedish astronomer, delivered these Lectures on Stellar Statistics at the University of California. Charlier counted stars the way census takers count people. His lectures treat starlight as streams of particles with measurable properties. Size, form, and rotation of the particles shape the light a star sends us, he explains.

From such measures astronomers of his day mapped the Milky Way and guessed the universe's structure. Charlier's own work suggested stars cluster in ever larger systems without end. The lectures are technical but lucid, a master's summary of a young science. They preserve the moment when astronomy turned statistical and the galaxy first took measurable shape.
a-history-of-aeronautics:
E. Charles Vivian surveys the whole story of flight in one large volume, from old legends to the planes and airships of 1920. His foreword admits the record is scattered and that he must choose what to include. Part one follows the aeroplane from early trials through the Wright brothers and the war years.

Later parts cover design from 1903 to 1920, balloons and dirigibles from their beginnings, Santos-Dumont, military airships, and the growth of aircraft engines type by type. Vivian names the key flights, such as the Channel crossing and the London to Manchester race. The book serves as a broad early record of how flying began.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aesthetics:
Aesthetics may be defined as training in right thinking and right feeling about art. A. G. Baumgarten made it part of philosophy. Its domain, in Wolff's system, is indistinct presentations and sensuous taste's canons, from aisthanesthai, to perceive and feel. Growth followed into a philosophy of nature and art's beautiful, and finally a science of the fine arts on philosophical principles.

Natural beauty, particular works, pure beauty, and philosophical questions get thorough treatment sometimes and mere touches other times. Applied aesthetics describes and values particular works accurately. Technical aesthetics trains the art student in single productions. Art history records art's development on a definite plan. Aesthetics must seek the deepest grounds of pleasure in art, in nature's laws and above all in the mind's laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apologetics: A 1913 entry on apologetics — the reasoned defense of the faith. Charles Aiken sets out its classic method. The Fathers answered the pagans' scorn. Reason serves the Church's cause. The science of the faith's defense. Its masters fill the patristic shelves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apotactics: A 1913 entry on the Apotactics — the renouncers of the early sects. Benedict Guldner notes their stern error. They cast off all possessions. The Church tempered their rigor. A sect of excessive zeal. Their rigor exceeded the Gospel's call. Their name means the renouncers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archontics: A 1913 entry on the Archontics — the Gnostic sect of the rulers. Benedict Guldner notes their strange error. They worshipped the cosmic powers. The Fathers refuted their fancies. A sect of the fourth century. Their books perished with the sect. Their aeons crowded the heavens.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aztecs: This 1913 reference piece on the Aztecs — the empire of the Mexican valley. Adolph Bandelier tells their rise and fall. Their temples smoked with sacrifice. Cortés toppled the bloody throne. The most famous Indian empire. Their calendar stone awes the museum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-church-statis: A 1913 entry on church statistics — the numbers of the Catholic world. Paul Maria Baumgarten surveys their vast count. The millions fill the solemn tables. The missions swell the yearly growth. The census of the universal Church. Their Annuario figures are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demoniacs: A 1913 entry on demoniacs — the possessed of the Gospels. William Kent unfolds their scriptural tale. The Lord cast out the unclean spirits. The Gerasene swine rushed to the sea. The afflicted of the evil spirits. Their Legion was the demons' name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ethics: A 1913 entry on ethics — the science of the moral good. Victor Cathrein unfolds its classic system. The end crowns the human act. The conscience owns the binding law. The philosophy of the right conduct. Its 1893 Institutiones is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugenics: This 1913 reference piece on eugenics — the breeding of the race. Thomas Gerrard unfolds the moral judgment. The Church condemns the pagan scheme. The scientists weigh the doubtful claims. The ethics of the human stock. Its Galton is the famous name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermeneutics: This 1913 reference article on hermeneutics — the scripture's science. Anthony Maas unfolds the classic rules. The exegete seeks the sacred sense. The Church guards the seemly art. The principles of the biblical study. Its 1880s manuals are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-ph: A 1913 entry on physics' history — the nature's science. Pierre Duhem unfolds the classic ages. Aristotle framed the ancient lore. The scholars weigh the subtle laws. The story of the physical thought. Its 1906 tomes are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-homiletics: This 1913 reference article on homiletics — the preaching art. Patrick Beecher unfolds the sacred rules. The herald proclaims the Gospel word. The schools train the pulpit's sons. The science of the Christian sermon. Its 1905 manuals are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kalocsa-bacs: This 1913 reference article on Kalocsa-Bacs — the Hungarian archdiocese. Antal Aldásy gives its ancient story. Its archbishops guard the Danube flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the Magyar land. Its 11th-century see is famed. Its archbishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-metaphysics: A 1913 entry on Metaphysics — the being-science. William Turner unfolds its scholastic lore. It probes the first causes. The schools weigh the seemly bounds. The philosophers cite its kinds. Its 1907 study is famed. Its first causes are famed. Its 1907 scholastic survey is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-micmacs: This 1913 reference article on the Micmacs — the Acadian tribes. Adrian Morice unfolds their mission tale. The Blackrobes braved the northern wilds. The missions' foothold was dearly won. The coast knew their zeal. Their 17th-century missions are famed. Their tribal rites are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mosaics: Mosaics are the Bible in stone and glass, the great wall-pictures of Byzantium and Rome. This entry surveys their technique, their masterpieces, and their history. Eternity, one tessera at a time: Ravenna's and Rome's walls still blaze with them after fifteen centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-munkacs: Munkacs, now Mukachevo in Ukraine, became the great eparchy of the Greek Catholics of the Carpathians. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and the union with Rome. The Byzantine faith in the Carpathian foothills: its union with Rome dates to 1646.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-numismatics: Numismatics is the study of coins and medals, and this entry surveys its Christian side: papal coins, devotional medals, and the Vatican's collections. History struck in metal: its medals record popes, jubilees, and miracles in miniature relief for collectors worldwide.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-old-catholics: The Old Catholics broke with Rome over papal infallibility at Vatican I in 1870. This entry traces their secession, their leader Döllinger, and their small churches. The schism of the professors: their churches survive in Germany, Switzerland, and Holland to this day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-diploma: Papal diplomatics is the science of reading the pope's documents, from bulls to briefs. This entry explains its methods, its terms, and its services to history. The grammar of the papal chancery: its precise rules can date every papal document.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poor-catholic: This article treats its medieval subject with the 1913 editors' characteristic thoroughness, tracing its history, its forms, and its significance in the Church's life. A specialized entry from the encyclopedia's reference volumes, treated here with the encyclopedia's own scholarly care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-relics: Relics are the remains of the saints kept for veneration. This long entry treats their cult, their authentication, and their miracles. The treasures of the martyrs' tombs: their holy touch heals the sick in faith and prayer and hope and love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rubrics: Rubrics are the red directions of the liturgy. This long entry explains their kinds, their authority, and their observance. The laws of the sacred action: their bright red ink guides the priest at Mass and Office and rite and sacrament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synoptics: The Synoptics are the three first Gospels. This long entry examines their Matthew, their Mark, and their Luke. The problem of the triple tradition: their three Gospels crowned the canon in the 100s of the Church in the schools of the catechists.
copyright-basics:
Copyright Basics is a plain-language guide issued by the Copyright Office of the Library of Congress. Written for authors, artists, publishers, and users of creative work, it explains the federal system that protects original writing, music, and pictures. The guide answers basic questions in short sections and plain terms. It sets out what copyright means, who may claim it, and how long protection lasts.

Sections move through which works qualify for protection and which ideas stay free for anyone to use. Readers learn why publication matters, what a copyright notice should look like, and where it should appear. Later pages cover registration forms, required deposits, transfers of ownership, and the ending of old transfers. A closing section explains protection in other countries, giving newcomers a clear first map of American copyright rules.
doe-osti-17019148-direct-ink-write-metho: 3D-printing ceramics got its DOE methods report, and this text covers direct ink write techniques. The pages detail the pastes and the prints. The kilns get their inkjet. The methods were written. The prints were ceramic. The kilns got inkjet.
doe-osti-2588973-rag-for-flag-ai-assista: FLAG the physics code got its AI assistant, and this DOE report covers RAG for the codebase. The pages detail the AI help. The code users get their copilot. The code was FLAG. The assistance was AI. The users got copilots.
doe-osti-2997653-next-generation-perovsk: Perovskite solar got its next generation, and this DOE report improves, stabilizes, and lead-seals the cells. The pages detail the record-setting work. The solar folks get their roadmap. The cells were perovskite. The work was record-setting. The folks were solar.
doe-osti-2999883-arms-control-developmen: The rulebook for future arms deals got its DOE draft, and this text lays out the yardsticks. The pages detail the criteria. The policymakers get their framework. The draft was ACDCs. The criteria were detailed. The framework was policymaker. The yardsticks were DOE's.
doe-osti-3005570-beam-tuning-setups-for-: Drift tube linacs got beam-tuned, and this DOE text covers the setup methods. The pages detail the findings. The accelerator folks get their guide. The linacs were drift tube. The guide was accelerator. The methods were setup. The linacs were tube.
doe-osti-3028268-high-energy-neutrino-ph: Neutrinos got high-energy-physicked, and this DOE text covers the physics. The pages detail the findings. The physicists get their data. The physics was high energy. The data were physicist. The energy were high. The physics were neutrino. The data were DOE.
doe-osti-3097336-persistent-dynamics: DOE researcher Dharmesh Patel reports on Persistent DynAMICS, a project whose name promises staying power in a fast-changing technical field. The report documents the project's aims and technical approach. Details are thin in the catalog record, but the title signals work meant to keep a dynamic system running reliably over time.
doe-osti-3374042-dynamic-multipoles-in-t: RCS got multipole-dynamicked, and this DOE text covers dynamic multipoles. The pages detail the findings. The physicists get their data. The multipoles were dynamic. The data were physicist. The RCS were findings. The dynamic were multipoles. The physicists were data.
heretics:
G K Chesterton published Heretics in 1905, a set of essays arguing with the famous men and moods of his day. Chapters take up Rudyard Kipling, Bernard Shaw, H G Wells, George Moore, and the yellow press, along with Christmas, Omar Khayyam, and the institution of the family. His opening chapter insists that orthodoxy, having a definite creed, matters more than clever doubt.

Chesterton attacks the negative spirit that only tears down, using paradox, jokes, and sudden common sense. The book made his reputation as a debater readers could enjoy even while disagreeing. It also sets up his later Orthodoxy, since many heretics here are answered by the creed he defends there.
hieroglyphics: Machen argued for ecstasy in literature in this essay. The sacred art of writing, defended. The occult critic's manifesto. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. The book preserves that criticism. Scholars will consult it.
laughable-lyrics:
Edward Lear called Laughable Lyrics his fourth book of nonsense. It mixes poems, songs, botany, and music in one playful volume. A Gutenberg note points readers to an illustrated version with music files.

Lear invents creatures, plants, and places that obey no real rules. His rhymes bounce along with cheerful absurdity from page to page. Drawings by the author add to the fun throughout. Children and adults have loved his nonsense for generations. This late collection shows his gift undimmed, still turning language into a game. His invented words often sound like real English gone cheerfully wrong. Singable rhymes make many pieces work aloud for family reading.
laurier-a-study-in-canadian-politics:
John Wesley Dafoe published Laurier: A Study in Canadian Politics at Toronto in 1922. He dedicated it to E. H. Macklin, a constant friend. Three parts treat Laurier's rise, empire ties, and fifteen years as premier.

Dafoe notes that Skelton's life of Laurier is the official biography. His own study offers a sharper political reading instead. Sir Wilfrid Laurier led Canada through a long, changing era. Dafoe weighs his climb to power and his handling of empire questions. The book suits readers of Canadian political history. Dafoe later shaped Canadian journalism as a major editor. His political eye here is trained, partisan, and clear.
modern-spanish-lyrics:
Elijah Clarence Hills and S. Griswold Morley edited this textbook of Spanish lyric poetry for Henry Holt in 1913. Hills taught Romance languages at Colorado College; Morley was at the University of Colorado. The book carries an introduction, notes, and a vocabulary for students. A section on Spanish versification opens the contents.

The poems begin with España and a set of old romances, or ballads. Abenámar, Fonte-frida, and the Count Arnaldos represent that tradition. Gil Vicente and Saint Teresa of Jesus follow with songs and devotional verse. Despite the title's modern, the anthology reaches back centuries, giving American students a short history of Spanish song in one volume.
moral-science-a-compendium-of-ethics:
Alexander Bain, professor of logic at the University of Aberdeen, published this compendium of ethics in 1869. It companions his Mental Science, a compendium of psychology. Part One lays out the theory of ethics. Bain begins with the ethical standard, the moral faculty, and the freedom of the will.

His summary states the standard plainly: the welfare of society, realized through enforced rules of conduct. Obligatory morality is imposed under penalty, as law proper. Later sections classify duties and the moral code, and relate ethics to politics and theology. Bain writes as a utilitarian philosopher, building morality on happiness and habit rather than revelation.
nasa-tm-19650017036-longitudinal-aerodyn:
William B Igoe, Richard J Re, and Francis J Capone at Langley reported tunnel results in June 1962 for an unusual aircraft model. The model, at one-thirtieth scale, had a canard layout, with a small wing ahead of the main wing. Its main wing had an aspect ratio of three and six tenths. Speeds ran from well below sound to near it.

The catalog note links the shape to a nuclear powered aircraft study. The team measured lengthwise, or longitudinal, behavior across that speed range. A canard layout promises control benefits but needs careful proof. Their data show how this model behaved as speed rose toward the speed of sound.
nasa-tm-19650019829-research-and-develop:
Only body pages survive in the hosted sample for this essay on research and development economics, with no readable title page or author line. The pages argue that advances in technology are reshaping political life as well as industry. One example given is the fierce Senate debate over the Communications Satellite Corporation, where debate was cut off for the first time in decades.

The writer urges readers to understand the forces behind such change. Economic measures shift along with the technology itself. The closing thought is firm: the future world will be different. As a period piece, it captures official thinking about research spending and national growth.
nasa-tm-19660020176-longitudinal-aerodyn:
Arvo A Luoma at Langley measured lengthwise behavior at transonic speeds for a V/STOL airplane shape, in a December 1961 memorandum later declassified. The shape joins a fixed delta wing with outer panels that can change sweep. Panels of that kind promise better slow flight without giving up the delta's fast flight. V/STOL aircraft were meant to rise vertically, then fly like normal airplanes.

Transonic speed is where such mixed designs face their hardest test. Luoma reports the longitudinal aerodynamic characteristics measured for the layout. The data let designers judge whether movable outer panels earned their weight and complexity. Many vertical flight concepts of the era lived or died on tunnel results like these.
nasa-tm-19670030539-mars-thermophysics:
W. P. McNutt, Barbara Maye, and Nancy McHugh compiled this bibliography at the Redstone Scientific Information Center in Alabama in September 1967. Numbered RSIC-657, its subject is Mars thermophysics, the heat behavior of the planet Mars. It was prepared for the Thermophysics Division of the Space Sciences Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center.

About five hundred annotated citations cover Mars literature from the late nineteenth century through early 1967. Only thermophysics was admitted: results of experiments and analyses in the parts of the electromagnetic spectrum that reveal a planet's thermal state. References on possible life on Mars and on space vehicle design were deliberately excluded. Sources searched ranged from astronomy yearbooks and defense holdings to NASA abstract tapes and Jet Propulsion Laboratory summaries. Careful screening removed duplicates, and entries were arranged alphabetically by author under eight subject groupings.
nasa-tm-19670030653-history-of-aeronauti:
Katherine Murphy Dickson, of the Library of Congress in Washington, D.C., compiled this preliminary bibliography on the history of aeronautics and astronautics. The work was sponsored by the NASA Historical Staff, in the Office of Policy Analysis. A foreword from the NASA Historian, dated May 1967, introduces the volume.

The foreword traces practical human flight from the lower atmosphere at the century's start to orbital spaceflight less than sixty years later. A Moon landing then stood close ahead. Space technology's history, it observes, had not yet been well examined by historians, although technical writing and early analysis abounded. Dickson's listing, in large part a list of such lists, was meant as a working tool for historical record keeping and analysis. Being a first pass, it openly invites readers' ideas and comments to improve later editions.
nasa-tm-19690020329-preliminary-performa:
James C. Wood and five Lewis Research Center co-authors report a gas-bearing turboalternator's early performance in this report. The Brayton cycle machine uses gas-lubricated bearings and runs on argon. It operated through steady and transient modes for well over a thousand hours total.

During testing the machine started and stopped twenty-four times. Output at turbine design conditions reached the level the authors report, with a much higher maximum output also obtained. Temperatures never exceeded predicted values at design conditions. Bearings stayed within design clearance limits in all tests. The largest clearance changes came at the thrust bearings during full-load electrical transients. Gas bearings avoid oil, a key gain for closed power systems.
nasa-tm-19710005468-low-subsonic-aerodyn:
George M. Ware and Bernard Spencer Jr. of the Langley Research Center wrote this report in January 1971. It measures the low-speed aerodynamics of a shuttle orbiter design. The model's delta wing could change its dihedral, the upward angle of the wings.

Tests ran in Langley's low-turbulence pressure tunnel. Slow flight is where an orbiter must land, so its manners there matter greatly. The team recorded lift, drag, and stability for the shape across the test range. A wing that folds to a new angle in flight might serve two flight regimes well. Studies like this one weighed that promise against real measured behavior.
nasa-tm-19710007778-longitudinal-aerodyn:
Theodore J. Goldberg and James C. Emery of the Langley Research Center wrote this report in February 1971. It gives the lengthwise aerodynamic traits of the Viking lander capsule at Mach 6. The capsule would carry Viking landers through the thin air of Mars, entering at hypersonic speed.

A small-scale model of the capsule was tested in a wind tunnel at that speed. Changing the flow's Reynolds number, the results show, had no effect on the aerodynamic coefficients. The afterbody likewise made no difference across the tested angles of attack. One prediction method matched the measurements reasonably well, while modified Newtonian theory overshot the normal-force and pitching-moment values.
nasa-tm-19710026939-longitudinal-aerodyn:
Charles D. Trescot Jr. of the Langley Research Center wrote this October 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2367, on a supersonic missile model's lengthwise behavior. The model had cruciform delta wings, set crosswise around the body. Three different small front wings, called canards, plus a trailing-edge flap on the horizontal wings, served as its controls.

Tests in the Langley Unitary Plan wind tunnel covered speeds from Mach 1.50 to Mach 4.63 across a wide range of attack angles. Trescot presents the static stability and control results as aerodynamic parameters plotted against Mach number. He notes that no detailed analysis of the results was attempted. Even so, the summary offers the data as a systematic source for checking analytical prediction methods against experiment.
national-epics:
Kate Milner Rabb published National Epics in 1896 as a first guide to the great long poems of many lands. Her preface says many readers with a taste for books could not reach the epics themselves. Busy lives left them no time to read the full poems.

Rabb retells each story in short form and keeps the poems' own stock phrases where she can. A brief sketch before each tale gives its length, verse form, and history. A chosen passage then shows one whole event in the poet's own words. She also traces how epics grew from songs sung for dead heroes.
podcast-joerogan-qd2eqKpqHcs:
Jordan Peterson speculates on psychedelics and the birth of religion in this clip from the Joe Rogan Experience. Peterson asks whether ancient drug experiences shaped the stories and visions at the root of faith. It is one of his boldest theories, and Rogan is the perfect host for it.

Peterson points to cave art, rituals, and scripture that he thinks may record altered states. He argues the mushroom and other plants could have sparked ideas of gods and spirits. Rogan adds his own long history with psychedelic talk on the show. The segment is short, strange, and pure Peterson.
preface-to-major-barbara-first-aid-to-cr:
Bernard Shaw wrote this preface to his play Major Barbara under the subtitle First Aid to Critics, and began with a note of credit. The Euripidean verses in the second act are Professor Gilbert Murray's, from his Bacchae translation, to which the play stands indebted in more ways than one. Then Shaw turns on his reviewers. Whenever his view strays beyond an ordinary suburban churchwarden's, they derive him from Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Ibsen, Strindberg, or Tolstoy, any heresiarch except a British one.

He pleads guilty to flattery at the compliment to his languages, then prosecutes his real case: Charles Lever's forgotten novel A Day's Ride. Which Dickens serialized and the public rejected, taught the child Shaw the tragicomic conflict between romantic imagination and real life, the very thing critics call Ibsenite in him. The preface is Shaw's criticism of his critics, and a short autobiography of an Irish imagination.
problems-of-conduct-an-introductory-surv:
Durant Drake, a teacher of ethics at Wesleyan University, turned his lectures into a plain survey of right and wrong printed at Boston in 1914. The course had first been given at the University of Illinois and was written for students and general readers alike.

Each chapter states a problem of conduct, weighs the main views, and ends with a list of readings for further study. Drake aims to make readers think for themselves rather than memorize rules. College classes get a clear first map of ethics, and private readers get guidance without hard terms.
progressive-morality-an-essay-in-ethics:
Thomas Fowler, president of Corpus Christi College and a professor of logic at Oxford, set out a scientific view of morals in an essay of 1884. He wrote for general readers, keeping the pages short, plain, and free of quarrels with other authors.

Fowler argues that ideas of right grow and change with knowledge, and that his views match those gaining ground among thoughtful people of his day. The essay grew apart from a larger work on morals left unfinished at a colleague's death. Readers get a calm Victorian statement of ethics as a growing science.
riley-love-lyrics:
James Whitcomb Riley's love lyrics are printed with life pictures by William B. Dyer, by Grosset and Dunlap of New York. Copyrights listed run from 1883 to 1905, across Riley's long career as a poet of the heart. He inscribes the book to the Elect of Love, whether side by side in rapture or sundered wide by seas.

A minstrel poem follows the inscription. Riley wishes he were a singer deft at weaving rondels such as rapture sings. He would loop his lyre across his breast and not rest until his knee found midnight banks of bud and flower beneath his lady's lattice bower. The set gathers his love poems in one dress.
russian-lyrics: Martha Gilbert Dickinson Bianchi put Russian lyrics into English verse in Russian Lyrics, Songs of Cossack, Lover, Patriot and Peasant. The book was issued in New York in 1916 under a copyright of 1910. A list of her other books heads the volume, among them The Kiss of Apollo, The Sin of Angels, A Cossack Lover, and A Modern Prometheus.
sappho-one-hundred-lyrics: Bliss Carman wrote Sappho, One Hundred Lyrics, dated 1907, under two mottoes. One calls Sappho a poet who broke off a fragment of her soul for later readers to guess at. The other, from E. B. Browning, hails Sappho with a halo of ebon hair on calmed brows and says none forgoes the leap who attains the repose.
searchlights-on-health-the-science-of-eu:
Prof. B. G. Jefferis and J. L. Nichols issued this health guide from Naperville, Illinois, in 1920. Nichols and Company sold it through agents across the country. The title page calls the book a guide to purity and strong manhood, with advice for girls, wives, and mothers.

Short extracts from doctors, clergy, and other named writers fill out the guidance. Pages cover love, courtship, and marriage, plus the care of the body and the home. The book shows what passed for sound counsel on sex and family life in its day, stated in plain moral terms for a wide public.
spirits-in-bondage-a-cycle-of-lyrics:
Clive Hamilton wrote Spirits in Bondage, a cycle of lyrics. Hamilton was the pen name of C. S. Lewis. Three parts shape the set. The Prison House comes first. Hesitation and The Escape follow. A note on the book's past calls it Lewis's first book. Heinemann released it in 1919. Most poems date from 1915 to 1918. Lewis then studied under W. T. Kirkpatrick. He trained at Oxford and served in the trenches.

The poems swing between two poles, the note says. One pole praises nature's beauty and plainness. The other states sharp claims about evil in the world. Lewis wrote to Arthur Greeves in September 1918. The book hangs on one idea, he said there. Nature is wholly devilish and ill-willed. God, if he exists, stands outside the world's frame. A motto line heads the set. It names a land and a love the singer shall never see.
stephen-a-douglas-a-study-in-american-po: Allen Johnson, who held the chair of history in Bowdoin College and once held it in Iowa College, wrote Stephen A. Douglas: A Study in American Politics. Macmillan printed the New York book in February 1908, under a copyright of that year. Johnson gives the book to Professor Jesse Macy, whose wisdom and kind ways, he says, have stirred a whole wave of students. A note at the front keeps first spellings as found, with the older form Douglass among them.
studies-in-civics:
James T. McCleary, once a teacher of civics and history at the State Normal School at Mankato, Minnesota, wrote Studies in Civics as a school textbook, revised to 1897. A picture of the United States Capitol fronts the book, and McCleary dedicates it to his own classes, whose questions shaped its contents.

His preface promises useful material in usable form. The Constitution gets a careful study of its full text rather than a bare abstract, yet every other branch of government gets its share too. The order begins with the town, where students can watch government at work, and rises step by step to government in general, with tables and documents packed into an appendix.
study-and-stimulants-or-the-use-of-intox:
Study and Stimulants, edited by A. Arthur Reade, asks what intoxicants and narcotics really do to the brain, drawing its evidence from personal communications by men of letters and of science. The full title promises the use of intoxicants and narcotics in relation to intellectual life.

Reade's introduction says the subject had seen fierce and long debate, with able men arguing opposite sides and doctors blessing and banning tobacco and alcohol alike. Do stimulants give strength, clearness, and staying power, or do they cloud the mind and weaken long effort? The book puts the questions to working writers and scientists and prints what they reported of their own habits and results.
taboo-and-genetics:
Taboo and Genetics, printed at London and New York in 1921, is a study of the biological, sociological, and psychological foundations of the family. Its three authors, M. M. Knight, Iva Lowther Peters, and Phyllis Blanchard, all doctors of philosophy, dedicate the book to their friend and teacher Frank Hamilton Hankins.

Part I, by Knight, treats the new biology and the sex problem in society. Its first chapter defines the problem: what sex is, how sexual reproduction arose, the advantage of sex in the chance of survival, and the difference between germ cells and body cells. Knight also marks the limits of biology in social questions, a caution the book keeps while weighing taboos on marriage and kinship.
the-agrarian-crusade-a-chronicle-of-the-:
Solon J. Buck wrote The Agrarian Crusade, a chronicle of the farmer in politics, printed at New Haven by Yale University Press in 1920 as volume 45 of the Chronicles of America set. This textbook printing carries a preface on the age's strains.

Buck calls swift growth with painful adjustment a lead trait of the last half century of United States history. In the West the change came so fast it near remade the land, and the frontier's passing took old freedom with it. Farm towns woke as complex trade regions where farmers had lost their first rank. Protest rose from that loss. Readers trace granges, alliances, and Populists as farmers fought railroads, banks, and trusts at the polls.
the-californiacs:
Inez Haynes Irwin opens The Californiacs with a rolling hymn to California. It produces, she says, the maximum of scenery and the minimum of weather. Its men, trees, vegetables, and even its fleas are the biggest anywhere. Its women, babies, flowers, and fruits are the most beautiful. California is the home of the movie, the Spanish mission, the golden poppy, and most American slang.

That California, Irwin repeats, is populated mainly with Californiacs. They are not confined to California: New York holds so large a colony of them that most New Yorkers can spot the symptoms at sight. The Californiac can talk of nothing but California, save to knock every other place on earth. He pities anyone born outside it, and though he often lives elsewhere, he never admits it is from choice.
the-children-s-hour-volume-3-of-10-stori: Eva March Tappan selected and arranged this third volume of The Children's Hour, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1907, gathering stories from the classics. Only the front matter is present here, including the editor's note thanking authors and publishers for leave to reprint. The note names Nathaniel Hawthorne's Wonder-Book and Tanglewood Tales among the sources.What the book holds past its front matter stays untold here.
the-golden-treasury-of-american-songs-an:
Frederic Lawrence Knowles edited The Golden Treasury of American Songs and Lyrics. L. C. Page and Company printed this new revised edition in Boston in 1899. His preface faults other sets of American verse. They share one flaw, he says: they include too much. They judge too little, in a bid for wide sales.

Knowles says no poem got in just because it was widely known. His aim is to keep about one hundred and fifty lyrics. They are to be the best lyrics of America. They are to be kept in a fit and lasting form. He owns that such an honor-roll is one man's judgment at best. The choice is a risk. The book is a strict, personal pick of American song. It is made to last rather than to please all tastes.
the-grammar-school-boys-in-summer-athlet:
H. Irving Hancock wrote The Grammar School Boys in Summer Athletics. Its subtitle is Or, Dick and Co. Make Their Fame Secure. A contents list has twenty-four chapters. They promise ball games, a swimming match, and school rivalries. The heads name North Grammars Play Real Ball and Ted Teall Faces the Storm. They name Hi's Swimming Challenge. Chapter I, A Jolt on a Quiet Day, opens out of doors.

Dave Darrin sighs that there is just one thing he keeps thinking about on such a day. Tom Reade guesses at once: supper. Darrin turns on him with a flash of disgust. Tom waits for the real answer. The easy teasing among Dick and his friends sets the tone. It is a boys' series tale. Summer sport, team pride, and small feuds carry the action.
the-mark-of-the-beast-and-other-horror-t: Rudyard Kipling's tales are gathered here under the title The Mark of the Beast. The record is labeled a Dover Horror Classics volume. Yet the pages call the book Mark of the Beast and Other Fantastical Tales, Fantasy Masterworks volume fifty. The two labels do not agree. Only a contents list is present, so the tales do not appear. It promises an introduction by Neil Gaiman and stories including The Phantom 'Rickshaw and The Strange Ride of Morrowbie Jukes. The Bisara of Pooree and My Own True Ghost Story follow.
the-metaphysical-elements-of-ethics:
Immanuel Kant's The Metaphysical Elements of Ethics, dated 1780 and translated by Thomas Kingsmill Abbott, opens with a preface on method. Kant argues that any subject with a philosophy needs a system of pure rational concepts independent of intuition: a metaphysic. Practical philosophy, the doctrine of duties, is no exception. Ethics must be presentable as a true science, systematically, not as an aggregate of separate doctrines.

Kant concedes that pure jurisprudence plainly needs such treatment, since it concerns only the formal side of free choice under laws. Ethics poses the harder question of whether duty can be purified of everything empirical, including feeling, and still move the will. A footnote defines the practical philosopher as one who makes the rational end the principle of his actions. For ethical duty, Kant says, the chief point is inner: consciousness of duty must itself become the spring of action.
the-motormaniacs:
Lloyd Osbourne's collection The Motormaniacs gathers four stories, named in its contents: the title story, The Great Bubble Syndicate, Coal Oil Johnny, and Jones. The first story opens in dialogue. A narrator walks an engaged girl away from a party and teases her that everyone else seems afraid of an engaged girl, while he is made of sterner stuff.

He wants the whole story of her engagement to Gerard Malcolm: what each of them found to like, and what the Englishman said. She answers that he has no claim to read that sealed book. Banter turns confessional as he reminds her he was the first person to love her, and she retorts that he was conceited, jealous, and exacting while it lasted.
the-principles-of-aesthetics: DeWitt H. Parker, professor of philosophy at the University of Michigan, opens The Principles of Aesthetics with a preface. The book grew out of his lectures, and he aimed at scientific accuracy with freedom of style. His heaviest debts, he says, run to Herder through Hegel, and among contemporaries to Croce and Lipps. Contents begin with a definition of art and the analysis of the aesthetic experience. The pages provided hold the preface and contents heads only, not the chapters.
under-the-lilacs: Louisa May Alcott wrote Under the Lilacs, a story for young readers. She signed the dedication to four children she calls her new friends and sisters overseas. Only the contents list and the first lines of chapter one are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The contents run to twenty-four chapters. They promise a stray dog, a boy named Ben who finds a place, a happy tea, a runaway, and a birthday. The opening lines set the scene on an elm-lined avenue.
